newsitem.title: BOSNIA: First German peace troops arrive in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: First German peace troops arrive in Bosnia.

text.p: An advance party of 120 German troops arrived in Sarajevo on Monday to join the NATO-led Stabilisation Force in Bosnia, witnesses said.
The deployment, part of the multinational peace enforcement effort in Bosnia, broke a post-World War Two German taboo on sending troops abroad in a potential combat role.
"The (Germans) are a part of headquarters staff rather than infantry," NATO Major Tony White said before the troops arrived at Sarajevo airport on a civilian Airbus jet from Cologne.
"What we are anticipating is another group coming in on January 14, again mostly headquarters staff and then the main body towards the end of the month," he told Reuters.

The German army will be sending the third largest contingent after the U.S. and Britain. It will include 2,200 infantry and armoured vehicle-borne reconnaissance troops equipped and trained for combat.

Bonn's troops will serve under French command, the first full-blown German army deployment abroad since World War Two when Hitler's Wehrmacht overran much of Europe, including Yugoslavia which included Bosnia at the time.
Germany's four-year occupation brought the Holocaust to Yugoslavia and inflamed a savage civil war which helped sow the seeds of this decade's conflict in Bosnia and Croatia.
Of the estimated one million people that died in Yugoslavia during World War Two, historians say the majority were killed by fellow Yugoslavs rather than the Germans.

Communist Partisans led by Josip Broz Tito and Serbian royalist Chetniks led by Draza Mihailovic took up resistance against the Germans and a puppet Croat-led Ustasha regime which slaughtered tens of thousands of Jews, Gypsies and Serbs.
The multinational Stabilisation Force has taken over from the Implementation Force (IFOR) to police the Dayton peace accord.

Bonn had about 4,000 troops in the IFOR mission whose mandate expired last month, but it limited their tasks to logistical jobs such as bridge building and running a field hospital, and they were stationed in Croatia rather than Bosnia to avoid any possible confrontations with Serbs.
After German unification in 1990, Chancellor Helmut Kohl took a series of small steps to lift the constitutional ban on German deployments abroad.
One reason was Germany's humiliation in 1991 when it paid $5.5 billion to Western allies fighting Iraq in the Gulf rather than send even a token force to aid in Kuwait's liberation.
